title: Netflix vs Blockbuster: Why Blockbuster Really Failed
description:
In 2000, Netflix's founders say they offered to sell the company to Blockbuster for $50 million, and Blockbuster said no. Ten years later Blockbuster was bankrupt, and Netflix now brings in over $45 billion a year. This case study follows Blockbuster's late-fee business, Netflix's no-late-fee subscription, the disputed meeting, Blockbuster's fight back with Total Access, the bankruptcy, and three business lessons you can use.

Accounts of the 2000 meeting differ: both Netflix co-founders describe a $50M offer that was turned down; Blockbuster's former CEO John Antioco says no serious talks took place. We show both.
The late-fee total for 2000 is an estimate: 16% (as reported by the Washington Post) x Blockbuster's 2000 revenue of $4.96B.

scenes.say: In the year two thousand, Netflix's founders say they offered to sell their company to Blockbuster for fifty million dollars. Blockbuster said no.

visual.label: the price Netflix's founders say they asked

scenes.say: Ten years later, Blockbuster was bankrupt. Today there is one Blockbuster store left on Earth, in Bend, Oregon.

visual.label: Blockbuster store left on Earth · Bend, Oregon

scenes.say: And Netflix? Last year it brought in over forty-five billion dollars in revenue. That's more than seven times Blockbuster's best year ever.
So how did a small, money-losing startup beat a giant? And what does it teach you about money and business? Let's break it down.

visual.title: Netflix vs Blockbuster
visual.sub: the deal that wasn't, and what it teaches

scenes.say: Chapter one. The giant.

At its peak in two thousand four, Blockbuster had about nine thousand one hundred stores across the US and twenty-four other countries, around eighty-four thousand employees, and just over six billion dollars in revenue.
The model was simple. You drove to the store, picked a movie off the wall, and rented it for a few nights. Then you drove back to return it. And if you were late, you paid extra.

visual.title: How renting worked
visual.label: Pay a fee
visual.sub: drive there · pick a movie · drive back

scenes.say: Those late fees were a big deal. Blockbuster's own filing shows that in early nineteen ninety-nine, late fees were sixteen percent of its revenue. The Washington Post reported the same share for the year two thousand.
Sixteen percent of about five billion dollars is nearly eight hundred million dollars. In one year. From people who brought a movie back late.
And customers hated them. Blockbuster's own annual report later called late fees its most common customer complaint, in its words, the most prevalent one.

visual.source: Blockbuster 2006 annual report (10-K), on late fees

scenes.say: Chapter two. The upstart.

Netflix was founded in nineteen ninety-seven by Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph. Its website launched in April nineteen ninety-eight, renting DVDs by mail. The monthly subscription came in September nineteen ninety-nine.

You may have heard Hastings started Netflix after a forty dollar late fee for Apollo Thirteen. He has told that story. But his co-founder, Marc Randolph, calls it a convenient fiction. The real start was two entrepreneurs looking for something to sell online.
The subscription was the real idea. For nineteen dollars and ninety-five cents a month, you could keep three DVDs at a time. No due dates. No late fees. No shipping charges.

visual.label: a month · 3 DVDs out at a time
visual.sub: no due dates · no late fees · no shipping charges

scenes.say: Think about what that did. Keep a movie as long as you like. Send it back when you're ready, and the next one arrives. Netflix still gets paid every month. The customer's biggest annoyance became the selling point.

But Netflix was tiny. At the end of two thousand, it had about two hundred and ninety thousand subscribers and around thirty-six million dollars in revenue. Tiny next to Blockbuster, and still losing money.
Chapter three. The meeting.
In two thousand, Hastings and Randolph flew to Blockbuster's headquarters in Dallas. Hastings later wrote that, walking in, he whispered: Blockbuster is a thousand times our size.

visual.label: "Blockbuster is a thousand times our size"

scenes.say: By revenue, it was more like a hundred and forty times. Still enormous. Blockbuster had nearly five billion dollars in revenue and over seven thousand six hundred stores. Netflix had thirty-six million dollars, and no stores at all.

In both founders' books, the pitch went like this. Blockbuster buys Netflix. Netflix runs the online side under Blockbuster's name, and Blockbuster focuses on its stores. The price: fifty million dollars.
Randolph wrote that Blockbuster's chief executive, John Antioco, was struggling not to laugh. The answer was no.

visual.title: "No."
visual.sub: per Randolph's book, That Will Never Work (2019)

scenes.say: But accounts differ. Antioco has said he wasn't at any meeting where a sale came up. In his version, Netflix came to pitch a partnership and made an off-the-cuff offer to sell. No serious talks.
And to be fair, Antioco has a point. Netflix lost fifty-seven million dollars that year. Paying fifty million for a money-losing website, just as the dot-com bubble burst, looked risky.
So saying no to one deal wasn't the real mistake. What happened next was.
Chapter four. The fight back.

Blockbuster did fight back, and hard. It launched Blockbuster Online in August two thousand four. On January first, two thousand five, it dropped late fees at its US company stores. In November two thousand six came Total Access: rent online, and return the disc to any store for a free in-store rental.

events.text:
Total Access:
return by mail or store

scenes.say: Dropping late fees was expensive. In its own annual report, Blockbuster estimated those fees would have brought in four hundred to four hundred and fifty million dollars of revenue in two thousand five. It gave that up on purpose.

visual.title: Late fees Blockbuster gave up (its own estimate)

scenes.say: And it was working. By the end of two thousand six, Blockbuster had about two point two million online subscribers, against Netflix's six point three million. Antioco says that by early two thousand seven, the two companies were in serious merger talks.
Then, in January two thousand seven, Netflix quietly launched Watch Now, streaming on computers at no extra cost. It had about a thousand titles. Its DVD library had more than seventy thousand.
A thousand titles, on a computer screen. Easy to dismiss. That's how disruption usually starts: small, a bit worse, and cheap to try.

visual.text:
Disruption starts small,
and easy to dismiss.

scenes.say: Then the giant blinked. Antioco had clashed with his board, including the activist investor Carl Icahn, and in July two thousand seven, Jim Keyes replaced him as chief executive. That year, Blockbuster limited the free in-store swaps, and then raised Total Access prices.
Chapter five. The fall.

Watch the next few years. Blockbuster's revenue slid from about five and a half billion dollars in two thousand five to about four billion in two thousand nine. Netflix grew from under seven hundred million to almost one point seven billion.
The stores went too. From over nine thousand in two thousand four to six thousand five hundred by the start of two thousand ten.

In two thousand nine, Blockbuster lost five hundred and fifty-eight million dollars. Netflix made a profit of a hundred and sixteen million. Blockbuster's own filing warned of substantial doubt about its ability to keep going.

On September twenty-third, two thousand ten, Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy, with nearly a billion dollars of debt and some three thousand US stores left. Netflix, by then, said it had more than fifteen million members.

visual.label: Blockbuster files for bankruptcy · Sept 23
visual.sub: Sept 23 · nearly $1B of debt · Netflix: 15M+ members

scenes.say: In April two thousand eleven, the satellite TV company Dish won Blockbuster's assets at auction, with a three hundred and twenty million dollar bid. The company-owned stores were all closed by two thousand fourteen. And in March two thousand nineteen, when a store in Perth, Australia closed, an independently owned store in Bend, Oregon became the last Blockbuster on Earth.
Notice what didn't happen. Blockbuster didn't ignore the internet. It saw the threat, built a real answer, and then pulled back when that answer got expensive while the stores still made money.

visual.text:
It saw the threat.
Then it pulled back.

scenes.say: Chapter six. Netflix today.
At the end of twenty twenty-five, Netflix said it had crossed three hundred and twenty-five million paid memberships. Up from about two hundred and ninety thousand subscribers in two thousand.
Netflix even shut down the business that beat Blockbuster. It mailed its last DVDs in September twenty twenty-three, after twenty-five years. It replaced its own winner before someone else could.

visual.label: Netflix mails its last DVD
visual.sub: Sept 29, 2023 · after 25 years of DVD by mail

scenes.say: Here's one recent quarter. From July to September twenty twenty-six, Netflix brought in about twelve point nine billion dollars. After the cost of its shows and delivering them, marketing, technology and admin, about four and a half billion was left as operating profit.

That's an operating margin of about thirty-five percent, up from twenty-eight percent a year earlier, when a one-off tax charge in Brazil hit. About thirty-five cents of operating profit on every dollar of revenue.

visual.title: Netflix operating margin
visual.note: 2025 quarter hit by a one-off Brazil tax charge · Source: Netflix Q3 2025 and Q3 2026 letters

scenes.say: In that one quarter, Netflix brought in more than twice what Blockbuster made in its best full year.

visual.title: Revenue: one year vs one quarter

scenes.say: And that fifty million dollar price? At last year's revenue, Netflix now takes in fifty million dollars in less than ten hours.
Chapter seven. The lessons.

Lesson one. A customer's pain is an opportunity. Late fees were Blockbuster's most common complaint. Netflix built a business around removing it. Look around you: any fee people resent, or any wait they hate, is an opening for someone.

visual.text:
Find what customers hate.
Then remove it.

scenes.say: Lesson two. Don't protect a profit stream your customers hate. Sixteen percent of Blockbuster's revenue came from the thing people liked least. Giving it up hurt, so the company waited, and a rival without that baggage promised what Blockbuster couldn't.

Lesson three. Disruption starts small. Netflix began with a few hundred thousand subscribers and big losses. By two thousand nine it had about forty times as many. Streaming started with a thousand titles. Both were easy to dismiss, until they weren't.

visual.title: Netflix subscribers (millions, year end)
visual.note: Sources: Netflix S-1 (2002) and 2009 annual report

scenes.say: And for your own money: notice the fees you pay only because leaving is a hassle. Those are exactly the fees a competitor will remove. And when you look at any business, ask which of its profits depend on customers having no better option.

visual.title: Use it yourself
items: Spot fees you pay out of habit
Ask: which profits need no rival?

scenes.say: Netflix isn't guaranteed to win forever, either. It now competes with many other streaming services, and the same rules apply to it. Customers stay only while the deal feels fair.

visual.label: is too big
visual.sub: the same rules apply to Netflix
